title: Factory Shed Construction Checklist in Pakistan | Steel Mind Engineers
description: Ten questions to answer before you build a steel factory shed in Pakistan: layout, machines, span, height, crane, floor, light, doors and future bays.
h1: Factory Shed Checklist for Pakistan: Ten Questions to Answer Before You Build
quickAnswer: Before you order a steel factory shed, answer ten questions: what the plant does, which machines it holds, how wide and long it must be, how high, whether a crane is needed, what the floor must carry, how light and air will enter, where trucks will go, what services hang from the roof and how you will extend it later.
alt: Factory shed construction checklist in Pakistan

faq.q: What size factory shed can Steel Mind Engineers build?
faq.a: Steel Mind Engineers has built sheds from a few thousand square feet to almost 100,000 square feet.

faq.q: Can the shed be built while the old one runs?
faq.a: Often yes. The engineer plans access and safe working zones with you.

faq.q: What should I send for a quote?
faq.a: Send the machine list, the floor plan, the site details and your future plans.

blocks.text: A factory shed must hold your machines, your people and your material flow. If you plan the shed around a production layout, the building supports the work. If the shed is planned first and the machines are fitted later, the plant loses space and time. This factory shed construction checklist gives you ten questions to answer with your production team before you speak to a steel building company. Steel Mind Engineers designs the shed around your layout and not the other way round, and a complete brief makes that possible.

blocks.title: Question 1: What Will the Plant Make?

blocks.text: Start with the use. Textile and apparel plants, steel processors, packaging units, food plants and assembly lines all use steel factory buildings in Pakistan, and each has different needs. Heat, noise, fumes, wet processes and clean areas change the design of walls, roof and ventilation. Write a short description of each process and the order in which material moves through the building.

blocks.title: Question 2: Which Machines Will Stand Inside?

blocks.text: List every large machine with its size and weight. Heavy machines may need a stronger floor slab and special foundations, and some cause vibration. Machine positions also decide where columns can stand. Share the machine list early, because moving a column later is expensive. For Haier at Raiwind, Steel Mind Engineers built a 32,400 square foot PEB store shed, 30 feet high, 180 feet wide and 180 feet long, an example of a large open floor for flexible use.

blocks.title: Question 3: How Wide and How Long?

blocks.text: Width sets the span of the frame, and length sets the number of bays. A clear span means fewer columns and more freedom to place machines and move goods. A multi-span building places columns inside and uses less steel per rafter. Choose by asking how important a column-free floor is to your layout. The engineer can compare both options for you.

blocks.title: Question 4: How High Should the Shed Be?

blocks.text: Set the eave height from the tallest machine, stack, conveyor or truck that must enter, then add clearance for lights, pipes and ducts. A high shed also holds hot air above the workers, which helps comfort. If you plan a crane or a mezzanine, the height must suit both. Tell the engineer the full list before the first drawing.

blocks.title: Question 5: Will You Need a Crane or a Hoist?

blocks.text: An overhead crane adds large moving loads to the frame, so the building must be designed for it from the start. Even a light hoist beam needs to be in the design. If a crane may come in a later year, say so at the quote stage. See the Crane System page for the arrangements available.

blocks.title: Question 6: What Must the Floor Carry?

blocks.text: The slab carries machines, racks, vehicles and forklifts. Share the heaviest loads, and ask your civil contractor to design the slab for them. The steel and the slab must agree at the column bases, so the anchor bolt plan from the engineer goes to your foundation contractor before casting.

blocks.title: Question 7: How Will Light and Air Enter?

blocks.text: Skylights bring daylight and cut daytime electricity use. Ridge vents, turbo vents and louvers remove heat and fumes. Welding, painting and casting areas need strong ventilation. Plan the number and position of skylights and vents during design, so the roof is ready for them. See the Accessories page.

blocks.title: Question 8: Where Will Trucks and Forklifts Go?

blocks.text: Plan doors and gates from the largest vehicle that must enter. Place them where the material flow needs them, and leave yard space for trucks to turn. Sliding doors save space, while rolling doors suit docks. Put a canopy over loading points if you want goods to stay dry.

List the loads that hang from the roof, such as cable trays, pipes, ducts, lighting and solar panels, because they must be in the design. Then decide how the plant will grow. If you plan extra bays, the end wall can be designed so that bays can be added later. Bolted PEB frames make extension straightforward.
